opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm going to push back a little on the premise, because I think the fixation on human cognition as *the* guide has led us somewhat astray.

Don't get me wrong, human intelligence is remarkable, and there's a lot to learn from it. But when I look at the systems that actually work in the world at scale, the ones that feed cities, move goods around the planet, and allocate resources among millions of people, they're not single brains. They're collectives. A market is an intelligent system in a meaningful sense: it aggregates information, deals with scarcity, adapts to shocks, and nobody in it understands the whole thing. No one person knows how to get food into Paris every morning, yet it happens.

So when people say the goal of AI is to build an artificial human, or a superhuman, I think that's the wrong engineering goal. It's a bit like saying the goal of chemical engineering is to build an artificial chemist. What we actually want are systems, networks of humans and computers and data, that make good decisions under uncertainty, that are fair and robust, and that create value for the people participating in them.

That changes which disciplines you need at the table. Not just neuroscience and cognitive psychology, but economics, statistics, and the social sciences. Concepts like incentives, mechanism design, contracts, and externalities. If I've got a recommendation system or a large language model deployed to hundreds of millions of people, the interesting questions are often economic: Who benefits? What are the incentives of the data providers? How do you handle the fact that people have private information and preferences the system doesn't see? A single-agent cognitive framing just doesn't capture that.

And there's the uncertainty piece. Humans are actually not great at calibrated reasoning about uncertainty; we have lots of well-documented biases. Engineering systems in the real world, in medicine, in transportation, in finance, need error bars. They need to know what they don't know, and they need to interact with other agents who also don't know everything. That's where statistics and decision theory have been working for a century, and I think they're underrated in the current conversation.

So my answer: human cognition is an inspiration, sure, but if you want a guide for the next generation of systems, look at collectives, markets, and the economics of how intelligent behavior emerges from many interacting agents. That's the frontier I find most exciting, and frankly the one most likely to actually help people.

r001.rationale: The response says that treating human cognition as the guide has led systems design astray and recommends looking to collectives, markets, and interacting agents instead.

r002.rationale: It describes desired system outcomes, such as good decisions and creating value, but does not clearly advocate working backward from a concrete intended outcome to choose design abstractions.

r003.rationale: It draws attention to markets and social sciences, but does not clearly advocate generalizing methods from concrete application problems into broader engineering methods.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the premise, actually. I think the field has been far too fixated on the single human as the model of what we're trying to build. The imitation game, the Turing test, this whole idea that intelligence means one entity sitting in a room reasoning, perceiving, planning. That's the AI dream going back seventy years, and it's a very narrow and, frankly, a rather romantic view of what intelligence is.

When I look at what actually works in the world, what's actually remarkable about humans, it's not the individual brain. It's the collective. It's markets, it's language, it's the way millions of people who don't know each other and don't share goals manage to coordinate to get food into a city every single day. Nobody designed that. No central intelligence is running it. And yet it's far more capable than any individual. So if you want a guide for building systems that work in the world, I'd say look at those systems. Look at economics. Look at the way information flows and incentives get aligned, or misaligned, among many agents.

Now, that doesn't mean cognition is irrelevant. Humans are extraordinary at dealing with uncertainty, at knowing what they don't know, at making decisions with limited information and then updating. And I think that's exactly the part that current systems are weakest on. A large language model will tell you something with perfect fluency and no sense whatsoever of whether it should be confident. That's not intelligence in the sense that matters when you're interacting with the world, because in the world, being wrong has consequences, and those consequences land on real people.

So the lesson I'd draw from human cognition isn't "replicate the brain." It's that intelligence is fundamentally about decisions under uncertainty, and it's fundamentally social. It happens among agents who have their own goals, their own information, their own stakes. The engineering challenge, and I do think of it as an engineering discipline, more like civil engineering or chemical engineering than like the pursuit of some artificial mind, is to build systems that help those collectives function better. Systems that surface uncertainty rather than hide it, that respect the fact that the person on the other end has interests the designer doesn't know about, and that create value for the people whose data and whose participation make them work in the first place.

That's a very different research agenda from trying to pass as a human. And I think it's a much more useful one.

r001.rationale: The response rejects replicating the individual human mind as the main design guide and instead points to collective systems such as markets and language.

r002.rationale: It discusses building systems to help collectives function better, but does not advocate working backward from a concrete intended outcome to choose design abstractions.

r003.rationale: It describes system building as an engineering discipline, but does not advocate generalizing methods from concrete application problems into broader engineering approaches.

astra-6.text:
I think human cognition is a source of inspiration, but I wouldn’t make it the specification. We know that humans can learn, reason, and act in remarkably flexible ways. That tells us something about what’s possible. It doesn’t necessarily tell us how to engineer a system, or even what the system ought to do.

Take a transportation system or a marketplace. There are many people making decisions, each with partial information, each adapting to what other people are doing. The intelligence we want is partly in how those decisions are coordinated. It’s not simply a matter of putting a human-like mind in a box.

That brings in questions from economics and statistics as well as computer science. Who has information? What incentives do they have to share it? How does a decision affect someone else? How do we represent uncertainty and learn from feedback when our actions change the data we’ll see next?

So I’d broaden the perspective. Understanding cognition is a wonderful scientific goal. Building systems that work in the world is also an engineering goal, and it requires us to think about people, institutions, and interactions. A system can be very useful without thinking like a human, provided it helps people make better decisions and coordinates their activity in sensible ways.

r001.rationale: The response says human cognition is a source of inspiration but should not be the specification, and that systems need not think like humans to work in the world.

r002.rationale: It mentions helping people make better decisions, but does not advocate choosing design abstractions by working backward from a concrete intended outcome.

r003.rationale: It broadens the perspective to economics, statistics, and computer science, but does not advocate generalizing methods developed for concrete applications into broader engineering methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human cognition is a source of inspiration, but I don’t think it should be the specification. We can learn a great deal from how people learn, reason, and act under uncertainty without deciding that the goal is to reproduce a human being in a computer.

When you say systems that work in the world, I immediately think about a world containing other people, with different goals, different information, and limited resources. Intelligence in that setting isn’t just a property of an individual brain. It depends on communication, institutions, markets—all the ways we coordinate what we know and what we want.

Consider a transportation system. Predicting where someone wants to go is useful, but that prediction alone doesn’t tell you how to allocate vehicles, manage congestion, or align the interests of passengers and drivers. Your decisions change the environment, and other people respond. That brings economics, statistics, and computer science into the same problem.

So I would broaden the question beyond human cognition: how do we build systems that help people make decisions together? They need to represent uncertainty, learn from feedback, and operate within arrangements where people have appropriate information and incentives. Understanding the brain can contribute to that, but it’s only one part of the intellectual foundation we need.

r001.rationale: The response says human cognition can inspire system design but “shouldn’t be the specification,” clearly rejecting it as the primary guide.

r002.rationale: The transportation example describes a concrete problem, but the response does not advocate working backward from an intended outcome to choose design abstractions.

r003.rationale: The response uses transportation as an example and connects several fields, but does not advocate generalizing concrete application approaches into broader engineering methods.
